title: The Message Left Unsent
description: For six years, brand strategist Nikhil Verma keeps a single 428-word email in his drafts folder addressed to Ananya Sen in Montreal—editing it thirty-four times through promotions, heartbreaks, and silence, until he finally understands what it means to let someone go.
excerpt: The number (1) in parentheses next to the word Drafts had survived three laptop migrations, four operating system upgrades, and two relationship dissolutions.
author: Noble John Steeven
coverImageAlt: An open email draft window on a laptop screen beside an old green ceramic mug with a chipped handle, autumn morning light coming through wooden window blinds

storySections.chapterTitle: I. The Ghost in the Sidebar
storySections.heading: I. The Ghost in the Sidebar
storySections.body:
The number (1) in parentheses next to the word Drafts had survived three laptop migrations, four operating system upgrades, and two relationship dissolutions.

It sat there in the left-hand rail of my email client, between Sent and Spam, quiet and permanent as a watermark. Every email application has its own typography for unfinished thoughts: sometimes a soft slate grey, sometimes an italicized bracket, sometimes a persistent amber dot. In mine, it was a dull, utilitarian charcoal: Drafts (1).

If you clicked it, the subject line read: A few things from Ber Sarai (or, before you pack).

The timestamp in the metadata showed it was first created on November 14, 2018, at 2:47 AM, on a dented silver MacBook Air whose battery swelled until the trackpad no longer clicked. Over the following seventy-one months, it had been opened and modified thirty-four times.

The word count was four hundred and twenty-eight words.

I am thirty-four now. I work as a brand strategy director in a converted textile warehouse in Shahpur Jat, where young art directors with silver nose rings argue about the semiotics of oat milk packaging and client billings are tracked in thirty-day rolling retainers. I own two suits tailored in Khan Market, a collection of Japanese fountain pens I rarely use, and a second-floor flat in Chittaranjan Park whose balcony looks into the crown of a sixty-year-old neem tree.

I am, by every external metric of urban middle-class Delhi, a functional, self-contained adult.

Yet several times a month—usually around midnight, or at six in the morning before the milkman rings the brass bell downstairs—I would find my cursor hovering over that charcoal bracket. I would click it open. The familiar white rectangle would expand across the screen, holding the words like insects preserved in clear resin.

It was addressed to ananya.sen@mail.mcgill.ca.

The cursor would blink at the end of the final line: I don't think either of us was wrong, which is the only part of this I don't know how to forgive.

Beside it were two blue buttons: Send on the left, Discard Draft on the right. For two thousand one hundred and forty days, I chose neither.

storySections.heading: II. The Chipped Green Mug
storySections.body:
We met in the winter of 2014 in a damp, south-facing room on the second floor of a builder floor in Ber Sarai, two hundred meters from the southern boundary wall of JNU.

The room smelled of cheap floor disinfectant, damp wool, and the kerosene stove we used to boil eggs and muster up water for instant noodles. Ananya was doing her master's in development economics; I was in the English department, writing an incomprehensible dissertation on colonial administrative gazetteers that I would abandon nine months later for an entry-level copywriting desk in Okhla.

She was twenty-three then. She possessed a terrifying, practical clarity that made most people uncomfortable. While the rest of us sat at the Ganga Dhaba until two in the morning arguing about Gramsci and the peasant question over plastic cups of cardamom tea, Ananya would sit with her statistical tables and her blue Sharpie, cross-checking agricultural distress indices from Vidarbha.

'You talk in metaphors because you don't want to count,' she told me once, leaning back against the lime-washed wall of our terrace.

'Counting is boring,' I said.

'Counting is the only way you know if someone is starving or just complaining,' she replied, without looking up from her notebook.

Our domestic economy was centered on a heavy green ceramic mug we had bought from an itinerant crockery vendor outside the Munirka market for thirty rupees. The handle had a hairline fracture near the lower weld where I had dropped it on the stone sink, but if you held it with three fingers under the base, it didn't leak.

For three years, that mug was the vessel through which all our negotiations passed.

If she was working on an econometric regression and had not slept for twenty hours, I would place the mug beside her mousepad filled with black coffee and half a teaspoon of condensed milk. If I had spent seven hours staring at a blank Word document feeling the specific, claustrophobic panic of failing my comprehensive exams, she would set the mug in front of me with warm milk and crushed ginger, saying nothing, merely tapping the rim twice with her ballpoint pen before going back to her desk.

We did not have what people in novels call a tempestuous romance. We had something much more dangerous: we had complete convenience, mutual respect, and the unexamined assumption that the physical coordinates of our lives would remain coincident forever.

We lived in that room until the plaster peeled, sharing one wardrobe, one ceiling fan with a rhythmic squeak in its bearings, and one key on a brass ring that we hid under the doormat when either of us went to the library.

When you build an intimacy out of routine rather than drama, you never notice when the foundations begin to shift, because the routine continues long after the faith has expired.

storySections.chapterTitle: III. The November of the Fog
storySections.heading: III. The November of the Fog
storySections.body:
The rupture arrived in the autumn of 2018, disguised as an official letter with an embossed maple leaf in the header.

Ananya had been awarded a doctoral fellowship in ecological economics at McGill University in Montreal—four years of fully funded research on carbon pricing models in sub-Arctic watershed communities, with a stipend that was three times what my advertising agency was paying me as an associate copy supervisor.

She told me on a Thursday evening in Hauz Khas Village.

We were sitting on the terrace of an old café overlooking the 14th-century water tank. The November smog had descended upon Delhi like a wet wool blanket, trapping the smoke of burning paddy fields from Punjab and the carbon fumes of four million two-wheelers. The medieval monument across the water looked like a charcoal sketch smudged by a thumb.

She took the printout from her canvas tote bag and set it on the glass table between us.

I read the first three lines: Dear Ms. Sen, On behalf of the Department of Natural Resource Sciences...

My first reaction was pride—genuine, sharp, and clean. She had worked seventy hours a week for eighteen months, running simulations on university computers that crashed every four hours, skipping weekend visits to her parents in Kolkata, drinking bitter coffee out of that chipped green mug.

Then came the second reaction: the cold, subterranean calculation of geography.

'Montreal,' I said, resting my elbows on the metal table.

'Montreal,' she repeated. She was watching my fingers, which were turning an empty sugar packet into a tight accordion fold. 'Classes begin in January. The visa office says processing takes six weeks.'

'That's very fast,' I said.

'Yes.'

We sat in silence for twenty minutes. The waiter brought two cups of filter coffee that smelled of chicory. Around us, two tables of design students were laughing about an Instagram campaign, their cigarettes glowing orange in the descending dusk.

This was the moment. Looking back across six years, I can see the crossroads with the precision of a satellite map.

There were two sentences available to me in the English language:

Option A: I want you to go, but I want to come with you. Let me look for copy jobs in Canada, or let's figure out how to bridge the four years.

Option B: Please don't go. Stay here. We will find an institute in Delhi or Bangalore. What we have between us is worth more than a paper on sub-Arctic watersheds.

I spoke neither.

Instead, governed by that peculiar, poisonous modern vanity that confuses emotional cowardice with intellectual maturity, I smiled a generous, civilized smile, tapped the table with my knuckle, and said:

'It's an incredible fellowship, Ananya. You have to take it.'

She looked at me for a long time. Her face did not register relief, nor did it register gratitude. Her dark eyes, magnified slightly behind her tortoiseshell spectacles, looked through my smile to the hollow space behind my ribs.

'You're not going to ask me to stay?' she said softly.

'I would never ask you to compromise your career for me,' I said, feeling noble, righteous, and completely dead inside.

She gave a small, dry laugh—a sound like dry leaves rustling under a shoe.

'You think you're being generous, Nikhil,' she said, putting the letter back into her bag. 'You're not being generous. You're just afraid of being responsible for what happens next.'

She stood up, paid her half of the coffee bill with a fifty-rupee note, and walked down the spiral iron stairs into the foggy alley.

storySections.heading: IV. The Sunday in Daryaganj
storySections.body:
Three weeks before her departure, on the first Sunday of December, we took the Yellow Line metro to Chandni Chowk and walked down Netaji Subhash Marg to the Sunday book market in Daryaganj.

The pavement market was at its winter peak. Two kilometers of second-hand books were laid out on plastic tarpaulins directly against the stone foundations of the Mughal-era city wall: Russian engineering manuals, three-volume editions of Will Durant, Victorian botany gazetteers, dog-eared Penguin classics sold for thirty rupees each.

The air was cold and smelling of roasted peanuts, exhaust fumes, and the sweet yeast of hot jalebis frying in mustard oil at the corner of Asaf Ali Road.

Ananya was looking for an old English translation of Georgescu-Roegen's The Entropy Law and the Economic Process—a text she claimed was out of print in India and cost eighty Canadian dollars in Montreal. She moved from one book pile to the next with the single-minded ferocity of a customs inspector, her fingers blackened with printer's ink and Delhi winter grime.

I walked beside her, carrying a cloth bag that grew heavier with every hundred meters: a collection of Agha Shahid Ali poems, an atlas of historical cartography, two detective novels.

At the third pile, near the Golcha Cinema, she found the book.

It was a 1971 Harvard University Press edition, bound in faded maroon cloth, its spine held together with clear packing tape. Inside the front cover was a stamp from the library of an engineering college in Roorkee that had discarded it forty years earlier.

She held it against her chest like a recovered relic.

'Look,' she said, turning the pages under the pale winter sun. 'Look at the margin notes. Someone worked through the thermodynamics equations in 1974 with a purple fountain pen.'

She looked up at me, her cheeks red from the north wind, her eyes bright with the genuine, uncorrupted ecstasy of discovery.

'You should write your name on the flyleaf,' I said.

She took a ballpoint pen from her coat pocket. She opened the front cover. Then she stopped. Her pen hovered two millimeters above the yellowed paper.

'What should I write?' she asked.

'Your name,' I said. 'And today's date. Daryaganj, December 2018.'

She hesitated. Then she wrote: Ananya Sen. Delhi / Montreal. Two cities joined by a single forward slash—a punctuation mark acting as a bridge, or a blade.

She shut the book. We bought two plates of chole bhature from a cart parked outside the cinema and ate standing on the pavement, balancing the paper plates on the bonnet of a parked scooter. The grease turned translucent on the paper; the steam from the chickpea gravy rose into our faces.

'When you come to visit in the summer,' she said, chewing a pickled green chili, 'we will take the train to Quebec City. They have second-hand bookstores inside old limestone vaults by the river.'

'Yes,' I said. 'In the summer.'

We both knew there would be no train to Quebec City. We both knew that Montreal in January was not an intermission in our shared narrative, but the beginning of a different book written in a language I did not speak. But we stood there on the cold asphalt of Old Delhi, eating spicy chickpeas, pretending that geography was merely an administrative detail that two people with university degrees could easily manage.

When we got back to Ber Sarai that evening, she put the book into the bottom of her black VIP suitcase, beside six packets of MDH garam masala and an electric kettle her mother had bought in Gariahat.

The room was half-empty already. Her bookshelves were bare; the nails on the wall where she had hung her calendar showed grey rings of plaster dust.

I sat on the edge of the mattress and watched her pack. I did not offer to help. To touch her clothes was to participate in her departure, and I was still determined to remain an innocent bystander at my own eviction.

storySections.chapterTitle: V. The Anatomy of What Was Deleted
storySections.heading: V. The Anatomy of What Was Deleted
storySections.body:
The draft was born three nights before her flight to Montreal, at 2:47 AM on November 14, 2018.

Over the six years that followed, the document became an accidental archeological excavation of my own ego.

In Version 1 (November 2018), it was six hundred and twelve words long—a sprawling, breathless manifesto written in the third gear of panic. It contained lines like: I haven't slept since Thursday. The flat in Ber Sarai feels like a crime scene. I don't know why I pretended I was okay with you leaving. It was desperate, unedited, and entirely honest.

I didn't send it because I told myself she was packing, that her parents were staying with her at the airport hotel, that burdening her with my eleventh-hour remorse was selfish.

By Version 7 (July 2019), eight months after her departure, the draft had shifted into anger. She had posted a photograph on Facebook of herself and four graduate students sitting on wooden Adirondack chairs beside a frozen river in Quebec, holding mugs of cider. They were laughing. She had cut her hair short—a sharp, asymmetrical bob that made her look like a French architect. She had never worn her hair short in Delhi.

I sat at my desk in Okhla and rewrote the draft into an indictment: It's fascinating how easily a life can be discarded when the funding is in Canadian dollars. I suppose all those years in Ber Sarai were just preliminary research on urban deprivation for your resume.

I saved that version. I kept it for three months. I didn't send it because, even in the depths of my spite, I knew the cruelty was an exact translation of my own humiliation.

By Version 18 (April 2021), during the second wave of the pandemic in Delhi, the draft transformed into terror.

The city was burning. The sound of ambulance sirens on the Outer Ring Road never stopped; every morning brought three messages in the family WhatsApp groups about oxygen cylinders and hospital beds. I had fever for nine days, shivering alone in my CR Park flat, drinking hot water and listening to the ceiling fan.

I opened the draft with trembling fingers. I deleted the anger. I wrote: Ananya, Delhi is dying. People are dying in parking lots. I don't care about 2018. I don't care about Montreal. I just want to know that you are alive and that if I don't wake up tomorrow, you know that the only time I ever felt entirely real was when we were sharing that chipped green mug.

I had my finger on the Send button. The trackpad was depressed halfway.

Then the fever spiked, my head ached with blinding ferocity, and I closed the lid. Two weeks later, when I recovered and the city began to breathe again, the email felt too theatrical, too melodramatic for the daylight of survival.

By Version 31 (November 2023), the email had been pruned down to four hundred and twenty-eight words of polished, museum-grade nostalgia. It was elegant. It sounded like an excerpt from an essay in a literary quarterly. It began: I was walking through the flower market at RK Puram yesterday and saw the small earthen lamps they sell before Diwali...

It was no longer a message to a human being. It was a monument I had carved to my own unresolved guilt—a literary performance for an audience of one who had stopped watching the stage half a decade ago.

storySections.chapterTitle: VI. The Photograph from Mile End
storySections.heading: VI. The Photograph from Mile End
storySections.body:
In September 2024, three weeks before my thirty-fourth birthday, the algorithm delivered its final verdict.

I was sitting in an airport lounge in Mumbai, waiting for a delayed late-night flight back to Delhi after presenting a rebranding pitch for a private bank. My phone buzzed with an Instagram notification: an alumnus from our JNU cohort had posted a series of photographs from a conference on global carbon governance held at Concordia University.

In the third slide was Ananya.

She was standing on the steps of a red-brick Victorian building in the Mile End neighborhood of Montreal. The autumn trees behind her were a blaze of scarlet, copper, and gold. She was wearing a heavy charcoal wool overcoat, a mustard-yellow knitted scarf, and leather walking boots caked with dry dirt from a field trip.

Beside her stood a tall man with thinning brown hair, wearing silver wire-rimmed glasses and holding a paper coffee cup with a Montreal bakery logo.

His left arm was around her waist—not the casual, polite grip of a colleague, but the settled, effortless possession of a partner whose body had spent hundreds of nights curled against hers.

On Ananya's left hand, resting lightly against the lapel of her coat, was a plain silver band.

She was not looking at the camera. She was looking at the man with the paper cup, her head thrown back slightly in mid-laughter, the cold wind blowing a strand of grey-flecked hair across her cheek.

It was a laugh I recognized instantly.

It was the laugh she used to produce in 2015 when the gas cylinder in Ber Sarai ran out mid-omelette, leaving us with raw eggs and two slices of dry bread. It was the laugh of absolute safety—the certainty that whatever catastrophe occurred, the person beside her was not going to smile politely and step out of the way.

I enlarged the image. I looked at her face for ten minutes.

There was no bitterness in her eyes, no shadow of old Delhi smog, no lingering grievance about a conversation on a rooftop in Hauz Khas. She had crossed an ocean. She had written her dissertation. She had built a career, learned French, bought winter boots, fallen in love with a man who drank coffee from a Montreal bakery, and married him in a stone house with an apple tree in the yard.

She was not waiting for an explanation.

She had never been waiting.

The entire seven-year drama of the drafts folder—the thirty-four edits, the late-night agonies, the carefully polished sentences about earthen lamps and chipped mugs—had taken place inside a closed room where only one person was present.

She had walked out of that room in November 2018. I had stayed behind, dusting the furniture and arguing with the curtains.

storySections.heading: VII. The Clean Inbox
storySections.body:
I returned to Delhi at three in the morning.

At 6:15 AM, when the first grey light began to filter through the neem leaves outside my bedroom window, I sat down at the dining table with a glass of water.

I opened the laptop.

There it was in the left rail: Drafts (1).

I clicked it. The window expanded. Four hundred and twenty-eight words.

Dear Ananya,

A few things from Ber Sarai (or, before you pack)...

I read the whole thing from the first sentence to the last. I read it not as an author, but as a stranger reading an old telegram found in a second-hand coat pocket.

The writing was very good. The metaphors were precise. The regret was balanced, tasteful, and thoroughly self-serving. It made me look sensitive, reflective, and tragic.

It was the most cowardly document I had ever produced.

To send it now would not be an act of love; it would be an act of vandalism. It would be throwing a handful of Delhi dust into a clean, well-lit room in Montreal simply to prove that I had once breathed the same air.

I moved the cursor away from the blue Send button.

I moved it to the right, to the small icon of the wire wastebasket: Discard Draft.

For seven years, I had treated that button like an executioner's lever. I had believed that discarding the draft meant discarding the memory—that if I deleted the text, I was conceding that what we had lived in Ber Sarai had meant nothing.

Now, with the morning sun turning the marble floor from grey to pale gold, I saw the truth.

Discarding the draft was not erasure; it was reverence. It was the only way to honor what had been real: by refusing to turn it into a tool for my own comfort.

I clicked Discard Draft.

A small dialog box appeared: Are you sure you want to discard this draft? This action cannot be undone.

I pressed Enter.

The white rectangle folded into itself and vanished.

In the left rail, the number disappeared. The text now read simply:

Drafts

No brackets. No count. Just an empty folder waiting for whatever the present day required.

I shut the laptop lid. I stood up, walked out onto the balcony, and leaned against the iron railing.

Down on the street, the vegetable vendor was pushing his wooden cart, calling out the morning prices of cauliflower and coriander in a rhythmic, chanting voice. The tea stall on the corner had lit its coal stove; a thin ribbon of blue smoke rose straight into the cool autumn air.

I felt a strange, cold lightness behind my ribs—the lightness of a man who has carried a heavy stone up a mountain for six years, only to realize he could have set it down at the first bench.

I breathed in the smell of woodsmoke, neem leaves, and diesel.

The city was awake. The day had started. And for the first time in six years, I had nothing left to say.
